title: The Cyclone...Insurance Policy
subtitle: Chapter 1, The Scam Behind the Curtain
body_html:
Not all my ideas are good ones. A little while back, I decided to start trying to understand the world of insurance. And then, when I tried to explain it to people like my wife, they got very bored. My wife, it's worth pointing out, is the chair of the insurance committee for the clinical TMS Society, so there's a degree of mansplaining that even highly excited and interested people just can't put up with. This is the problem with health insurance, it's endlessly complicated, but there aren't a lot of good characters. Instead of coming up with my own characters, I decided to borrow characters from the Wizard of Oz, because that's already agit-prop about the gold standard, so it shouldn't be too hard to turn into propaganda about health insurance. This is part one of that attempt. Yes, there's more. No, it's not much better; it's just as pedantic and silly as this part. Part of the problem is that the original Wizard of Oz is pretty pedantic and poorly written itself, so if you're doing a Pitch Perfect parody, it's still gonna be a little weird.

Thank you for putting up with my silliness. Without further ado, part one of my attempt to use the Wizard of Oz to explain health insurance in America….

Chapter 1: The Cyclone Insurance Policy

Dorothy lived on the Kansas Prairie. She was born there and grew up there. Dorothy is 19 years old; she just graduated from high school.  Her first job was working for one of the companies that moved to the Kansas City area.  It attracted many tech companies on account of its investment in high-speed broadband.  She was a simple country girl, and due to a tragic, Adverse Childhood Experience1, she was raised by her Auntie Em and her uncle, Henry.   Henry was stern, always solemn, and had a history of dark moods. 

Her family was farmers.  More precisely, they worked in the accounting department for Archer Daniels Midland (ADM).  They lived in a modest house with four walls, a floor, and a front door painted green. It had blazingly-fast broadband.  They led a simple life.   Uncle Henry had purchased the appropriate insurance policies to ensure they were indemnified against cyclones. They had whole life insurance, an umbrella policy, car insurance, homeowners insurance, and, through ADM, health insurance2. It was a “great policy,” according to the insurance broker who ran the open enrollment workshop for ADM.  “It's UnitedHealthShare; they are the best. You don't have to worry about anything!”

They lived on the outskirts of Kansas City, and in years past, not a tree or building broke the view from their home.  Their straightforward home, updated in the 1980s from its original farmhouse to bring it up to code, was painted a simple white. Now, of course, their home was surrounded by development.  They could see prefabs and businesses in every direction. The family couldn't help but notice many small medical practices had been acquired by a large hospital-based health system. Three of every four enterprises were medical: urgent care centers, pharmacies, and Moment Clinics.  Even the old Theranos Lab inside the Walgreens was now a Fibula Health OrthoStop.  Kansas must have a lot of people who care about their health!

As far as the eye can see, the slate-gray Kansas sky met the tops of buildings.  Those buildings were all gray, tan, or other earthy colors.  Drab and conservative was the color scheme of Kansas City.  The architecture was squatish and spartan.  It was often hard for the eye to tell where the Private Equity Leased Buildings for healthcare companies ended and the sky began.  Getting help, no matter what your problem, was easy.  Dorothy had no reason to worry. After all, the family had great insurance.  Uncle Henry had listed her as a dependent, so she would be on the ADM health plan until she had a “qualifying event” or turned 26 years old3.  It did seem a bit much to put almost half the household income towards insurance premiums.

Dorothy had a pet, Toto, the family dog.  Toto was a purebred dog and the pride of the family.  Unfortunately, Toto had the congenital hip dysplasia4 common in purebred dogs.  As a result, Toto frequently needed care at the Vet. Like most of the small businesses in Kansas City’s suburbs, Toto’s Vet was acquired as part of a private equity roll-up play in the “pet space.”  They also purchased supplemental pet insurance for Toto and his complex health needs.

Dorothy was new to the workforce.  Dorothy had big dreams. She worked at a Software as a Service (SaaS) startup.  Her role was as a customer support representative–but the high-quality fiber optic network made her home also suitable for work.  Some day, she would get out of the broadband-enabled suburbs of Kansas City, with its oppressive gray skies and endless focus on risk mitigation through indemnification.  Dorothy dreamed she would someday complete her studies to obtain a Master's in Public Health. Harvard University was far from the prairie, with its stern folk and midwestern values.  In Boston, well… that was the most prestigious Public Health degree in the land. These were dreams, and she held them close to her heart as she completed her chores in her midwestern home and updated her customer support calls in the company Slack.

But she was having trouble, and that trouble began to disrupt more than half the days of the week.  Sometimes she would have difficulty concentrating. A lack of appetite was also prominent, more than half the days of the week. Those gray Kansas skies seem to be in her mind as well.  She had a bad case of streptococcal infection last month. And, of course, she took an antibiotic. But three weeks later, she developed red spots all over her body.5  They itch. And they were a little bit scaly.  Dorothy began to worry. Over and over again, she would worry6. Was there going to be a tornado? Would the winds blow so hard there would be damage?  Would she be forced to file claims on their myriad insurance policies?  Would the carrier underwrite the catastrophe? Was she going to make a mistake on some of the paperwork? She checked their insurance policy documents, first just once or twice, to ensure they were there. Then she started reading them closely. Soon, she was all day going back and forth between scratching those little red spots and checking to ensure the insurance policies were in place.   The language on them indicated they were indemnified against any cyclones that could come their way.  So why was she so worried?

Auntie Em was a responsible adult, and she noticed Dorothy was suffering:

“My girl, my beautiful Dorothy, why don't you see the doctor? You've got those spots, and they weren't there before.  Of course, they do better when you're out in the sun, even though it blisters the paint on our home and makes it as gray as everything else in the Kansas Prairie.”

Dorothy spent the next week searching the internet.  She used matching platform after matching platform.  First, she would book an appointment with a dermatologist on FlockDoc.  Then, thinking better of it, she would try to find an in-network psychiatrist on Malma.  And she then used Listened.  And then Headstrong.  Then MindMatch.  Each time she used a matching platform to find an appointment, and each time the match felt…wrong.  Something wasn’t right.  It was hard to say what.  

The number of in-network options looked large at first7, but most weren’t accepting new patients8.  Many of the doctors weren’t accepting the insurance plans as listed.  Some had long waitlists9.  She couldn’t find the right match, and none of the algorithms were helping. 

Eventually, she booked with Dr. Skinman, which seemed like a…right name for a dermatologist.

1

According to large sample size studies, adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are an oft-overlooked contributor to morbidity and mortality.  In Dorothy's life, it was the death of her parents when she was young, in a freak tornado-related incident.

2

Health Insurance is a Tax Exempt Employee Benefit in the US thanks to a law called the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, or ERISA.  Every insurance law after that has been built on top of that law.  Therefore, compliance with ERISA is the name of the game in health benefits.

3

The ability to keep dependents on their parent’s insurance plan was added, up to age 26, in the Accountable Care Act (ACA).

4

Swenson L, Audell L, Hedhammar A. Prevalence and inheritance of and selection for hip dysplasia in seven breeds of dogs in Sweden and benefit: cost analysis of a screening and control program. Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. 1997 Jan;210(2):207-214. PMID: 9018354.

5

Streptococcus pyogenes, the group A Strep (GAS) bacteria, is the most common cause of bacterial pharyngitis– “strep throat” to most of us.  Our immune system utilizes a complex array of strategies to defend ourselves from a strep infection.  Starting with nonspecific defenses, our body deploys an army of white blood cells–Neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, and others to fight the infection.  Fighting a bacterial infection involves chemical warfare from our cells. They secrete inflammatory molecules that recruit more immune cells to the area in an inflammation process.  Our immune system tries to be very specific in its response. It's looking for proteins with particular shapes on the outside of bacteria. Strep has very similar proteins in the human body, so some of the response to infection–which to the strep started as a simple sore throat–can turn into a much larger problem. As a result, our immune system starts creating inflammatory responses against our bodies.  It's a case of mistaken identity, with human-body proteins mistaken for invaders.  And this can lead to chronic health conditions:

 Several inflammatory complications are associated with GAS pharyngitis, which can lead to chronic disease in patients. These include scarlet fever, tonsillar hypertrophy, and sleep apnea, as well as post-infectious sequelae, such as acute rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and guttate psoriasis.*

* Amelia T Soderholm, Timothy C Barnett, Matthew J Sweet, Mark J Walker, Group A streptococcal pharyngitis: Immune responses involved in bacterial clearance and GAS-associated immunopathologies, Journal of Leukocyte Biology, Volume 103, Issue 2, February 2018, Pages 193–213, https://doi.org/10.1189/jlb.4MR0617-227RR

6

For some, one of the symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder is the disconcerting feeling that something isn't right.  Obsessions are intrusive thoughts that cause distress.  You can be obsessed with a specific concern. The most familiar version is the obsession with being contaminated by dirt or germs. Still, it's not the quality or realisticness of the obsession that is the issue in OCD.  The disordered part of obsessing is the emotional distress associated with that intrusive thought.  If you're covered with dirt or bacteria, you might be contaminated. But the amount of distress associated with that worry is the disorder.  For some people, this comes with associated thoughts, like if “I'm contaminated, I could get sick,”  or “I might get other people sick.”  But in the case of many people, like Dorothy, it's not so much that there's a specific bad thing that's going to happen; there is often nonspecific distress. The feeling that something is wrong is nagging, even haunting.  It doesn't actually have to be attached to a rational or irrational thought. There can be no thought whatsoever. It can just feel wrong. And that feeling drives compensatory behaviors called compulsions.   A compulsion or ritual is an act or thought to neutralize the distress. These don't have actually to make any literal sense.  OCD is a brain circuit disorder.  With the checking and rechecking of doctor's appointments, Dorothy is beginning to get symptoms of it.

7

 One of the most significant problems in accessing appropriate medical care for mental health problems is the need for network sufficiency.  Although insurance companies usually have extensive listings of providers who are theoretically in the network, functionally, these are "ghost networks.”  The providers listed aren't those who will see you, could see you, or sometimes are even still living. Some of them are dead but still listed, and thus literal ghosts.  This is problematic.

8

The No Surprises Act of 2022, built upon ERISA, mandates health insurance companies keep an up-to-date list of providers in their network:

“The No Surprises Act requires all private health plans … to maintain accurate provider directories and requires providers to regularly update plans about any changes in their information. Plans must verify and update directories at least every 90 days and, on an ongoing basis, post any changes within two business days.”

9

Long wait lists for health appointments violate the Accountable Care Act (ACA) because they demonstrate network insufficiency on the part of the Health Plan. The ACA also follows ERISA – this is a big deal because tax-exempt status isn’t “free”-- it requires diligence on the part of employers.   Therefore, the ACA added specific guidance:

“The Affordable Care Act (ACA) requires … [that plans] ensure a sufficient choice of providers and provide information to enrollees and prospective enrollees on the availability of in-network and out-of-network providers.”

Coverage must be adequate. It can’t be theoretical coverage; it has actually to cover the care people might need. This, although obvious, turns out to be non-trivial. Federal oversight of adequacy returns in 2023. This includes quantitative measurements:

“Time/distance standards – This type of standard is used to determine whether participating providers are geographically accessible.”

It has to be close enough to your house. Further:

“Minimum number of providers – Another standard establishes minimum provider-to-enrollee ratios.”

There has to be a minimum number of providers for your problem. This minimum varies from locality to locality, but the minimum requirement is unlikely to be none whatsoever.

Also, the maximum wait time matters. That is another requirement. Behavioral health has its own specific limits here:

“Behavioral Health: 10 days (Source: 2023 Draft Letter to Plans participating in federally facilitated exchanges)*

There are other standards as well, as Dorothy will learn in her journey.
